# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems are designed. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62.4 pounds, and a column of water only one inch square but ten feet tall already exerts about 4.3 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure at its base. Engineers exploit this relationship constantly, because pressure in a water system is largely a matter of elevation: every 2.31 feet of vertical height corresponds to roughly 1 psi. Understanding this conversion is the key to understanding why your shower works on the twentieth floor.

## The Elevation Head: Gravity Does the First Push

Most city water systems begin with a reservoir or treatment plant positioned, whenever geography permits, at a higher elevation than the customers it serves. This is deliberate. If a reservoir sits 200 feet above a neighborhood, the water arriving at that neighborhood's pipes carries about 86 psi of pressure before a single pump has run. Engineers call this "elevation head," and it's free energy—gravity pushing water downhill through aqueducts and transmission mains.
